title: Sometimes Progress Means Taking Things Away
summary: People default to adding: more tasks, more charts, more code. What research on subtraction found, why deleting counts as progress, and how to spot weight worth removing.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Say nothing big happens on a Wednesday afternoon. No feature ships, no decision gets announced. But by 5 p.m. the sprint board has three fewer cards, because someone noticed they were the same task written three ways. A vague risk labeled "performance?" now has a clear name and an owner. And the thing everyone had been carrying around in their heads, "we're not doing offline mode this quarter," is finally written in the project doc. The work feels lighter, and everybody can tell.

We usually describe progress as addition: more output, more scope, more commits, more charts going up and to the right. Addition is easy to see, so it's easy to celebrate. Plenty of good workdays, though, get better because something heavy goes away.

We default to adding

There's research on why this is hard. In a 2021 Nature paper, Gabrielle Adams, Benjamin Converse, Andrew Hales and Leidy Klotz ran a series of studies, including eight experiments, asking people to improve things like a Lego structure, a mini-golf hole, a travel itinerary, an essay and a recipe. People systematically searched for things to add and overlooked changes that took something away. They were even less likely to find a helpful subtraction when nothing in the task hinted at it, when they had only one attempt, or when they were under heavier cognitive load (People systematically overlook subtractive changes).

The Lego task is the easiest to picture. Participants had to make a platform sturdy while it rested on a single corner block. Adding bricks cost money. Removing that corner block, so the platform sat flat on the layer below, was free and solved the problem. Without a hint, 59% bought and added bricks. When the instructions mentioned that removing pieces was free, that fell to 39% (Darden's summary of the study).

Look at those conditions again: no cue, one shot, a heavy mental load. That sounds a lot like a normal sprint. If the finding carries over to work, the busiest teams are the least likely to think of deleting something. The authors themselves suggest the additive default may be one reason people struggle with overloaded schedules and red tape.

What removal looks like at work

Removal rarely looks impressive. A question that kept coming up disappears because someone finally wrote the decision down. A noisy dashboard becomes useful because the team deletes the charts nobody trusts. A project gets easier to run because the owner says which part is out of scope. Someone sleeps better because a vague worry became a concrete risk with a next step.

In code it's even more literal. The simplicity chapter of Google's SRE book says every new line of code is a liability, calls code behind a flag that's always off "a metaphorical time bomb," and recommends removing dead code routinely. Its author, Max Luebbe, puts it plainly: "Some of the most satisfying coding I've ever done was deleting thousands of lines of code" (Site Reliability Engineering, Chapter 9: Simplicity). Fewer methods on an API, fewer branches in a function, one owner per ticket: less to understand means fewer ways to get it wrong.

Why it's hard to report

This kind of progress leaves little evidence. The board has fewer cards. The meeting is shorter. The design has fewer branches. The absence is the point, but absence is harder to put in a status update than activity. If your team only counts what got added, the person who deleted 2,000 lines of dead code looks like they did nothing all week. So say it out loud: "Removed the legacy export path, 2,000 lines, one less thing that can break." That's real work. (Prep work that prevents incidents has the same problem, covered in Why Good Preparation Looks Like Nothing Happened.)

Remove with judgment

Delete the wrong thing and you cause damage. Keep everything and you create drag. The skill is spotting what no longer earns its place: stale assumptions, duplicated work, unclear ownership, decisions nobody wrote down, rituals that continue only because they happened last month. Before you remove something, ask who depends on it and how you'd bring it back. Version control makes code easy to restore. A meeting, a process or a promise to a customer is harder to undo, so check with the people who rely on it first. Find the Way Back Before You Decide goes deeper on that.

Some weight isn't technical at all. A team stalls because nobody wants to say the plan is too wide. A person stalls because a task has no real definition of done. A review gets tense because the disagreement is really about who owns what. Naming that kind of weight often changes the room before any code changes. Removal also takes a little humility: admitting that some of yesterday's structure, maybe your own, isn't needed anymore.

Try this week

  • When the work feels heavy, ask "what could we remove?" before "what should we add?"
  • Archive duplicate or stale cards on your board.
  • Delete one chart or alert that nobody acts on.
  • Find one piece of dead code or an always-off flag and remove it, with a test showing nothing changed.
  • In your next update, list one thing you removed next to what you shipped.

faqs.q: Why do people overlook removing things as a solution?
faqs.a: A 2021 Nature study by Gabrielle Adams and colleagues found that people default to searching for additions and miss helpful subtractions, especially when nothing prompts them to consider removal, when they get only one attempt, or when they are under higher cognitive load. In their Lego task, 59% added bricks when removing one block was the cheaper fix; a reminder that removal was free brought that down to 39%.

Often, yes. Google's SRE book treats every new line of code as a liability and recommends removing dead code routinely, including code behind flags that are always off. Less code means fewer places for bugs to hide and less for the next person to understand.

faqs.q: How do I know what's safe to remove?
faqs.a: Ask who depends on it and how you'd undo the change. Code is easy to restore from version control. Processes, meetings and commitments to customers are harder to reverse, so check with the people who rely on them first.
